BST260 Final Project Proposal

Nicole Qin

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To: BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026

Project Overview

The objective of this project is to investigate two distinct public health questions using publicly available datasets. The project will apply data management, visualization, regression modeling, and model assessment techniques introduced in BST260. Particular attention will be given to data provenance, statistical uncertainty, model assumptions, and limitations of scientific interpretation.

Vignette 1: Association Between Body Mass Index and Systolic Blood Pressure Among U.S. Adults

Data Source and Study Population

The first analysis will use data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), available through the NHANES R package. The dataset contains 10,000 observations and 77 variables from the 2009–2010 and 2011–2012 survey cycles.

The study will focus on adults aged 20 years or older. Preliminary data exploration identified 7,235 eligible observations corresponding to 4,654 unique participant IDs.

Research Question

Is body mass index associated with systolic blood pressure among adults, after accounting for demographic and lifestyle characteristics? Does this association depart from a linear relationship?

Variables and Unit of Analysis

The primary exposure will be body mass index (BMI), measured in kg/m² and treated as a continuous variable. The primary outcome will be average systolic blood pressure (BPSysAve), measured in mmHg.

Age, gender, race and ethnicity, physical activity, and smoking history will be considered potential confounding or adjustment variables based on their plausible relationships with BMI and blood pressure.

The underlying unit of analysis is the individual participant. Repeated participant IDs resulting from the resampling procedure used to construct the NHANES teaching dataset will be explicitly considered.

Statistical Analysis Plan

The analysis will begin with descriptive statistics and exploratory visualization of BMI, systolic blood pressure, and relevant covariates.

Simple and multiple linear regression models will be fitted to investigate the association between BMI and systolic blood pressure before and after covariate adjustment. Natural cubic splines will be used to examine potential nonlinear relationships.

Model comparison, residual diagnostics, confidence intervals, and appropriate statistical tests will be used to evaluate model fit and uncertainty. The implications of repeated participant IDs will be addressed through appropriate sensitivity analyses, potentially including participant-clustered standard errors or survey-weighted analysis using NHANESraw.

Missing Data and Limitations

Among the eligible adult observations, BMI has 63 missing values (0.87%) and systolic blood pressure has 264 missing values (3.65%). The selected adjustment variables have no missing values in this subset.

Complete-case analysis will serve as the initial approach, with an assessment of potential differences between included and excluded observations.

Important limitations include the cross-sectional study design, residual confounding, measurement variability, repeated participant IDs, and limitations associated with the resampled teaching dataset. The estimated relationships will be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

Vignette 2: Temporal and Geographic Patterns of Waterborne Disease Outbreaks

Data Source and Study Population

The second analysis will use CDC outbreak surveillance data provided as the waterborne dataset in the finalproject R package.

The original dataset contains 66,713 outbreak records and 23 variables after conversion from a nested list into a tabular format. Restricting the dataset to records with water as the primary mode of transmission yields 3,106 records spanning 1971–2023, with no duplicated record identifiers.

The study will focus on reported waterborne disease outbreaks in the United States and will explicitly document the treatment of territorial and multistate records.

Research Question

How do reported waterborne disease outbreaks vary by month, calendar year, and geographic location? Do seasonal patterns differ across major categories of water exposure?

Variables and Unit of Analysis

The primary outcome will be the number of reported waterborne outbreaks aggregated within calendar months.

The primary explanatory variables will be month and year. Month will be treated as a categorical variable to examine seasonality, while year will be used to investigate long-term temporal trends.

Geographic location and water exposure category will be examined in secondary analyses. Categories will be defined consistently, with explicit handling of records involving multiple or undetermined exposure types.

The original unit of observation is an outbreak record, while the primary regression analysis will use aggregated year-month outbreak counts.

Statistical Analysis Plan

Descriptive statistics and graphical summaries will be used to characterize seasonal patterns, annual trends, geographic variation, and outbreak characteristics.

Poisson regression will be used to model monthly outbreak counts. The model will incorporate calendar month and year, with consideration of differences in month length and reporting coverage. Overdispersion will be assessed, and negative binomial regression will be considered if the Poisson variance assumption is inadequate.

Residual diagnostics, model comparison, and confidence intervals will be used to assess model performance. Potential temporal dependence and changes in surveillance practices will also be investigated.

Additional exploratory analyses will examine differences between drinking-water and recreational-water outbreaks. Outbreak size will be summarized using robust descriptive statistics because the preliminary distribution of reported illnesses is highly right-skewed.

Missing Data and Limitations

The filtered dataset contains no missing values for year, month, state, or the number of reported illnesses. Missing information in secondary variables, including deaths and water type, will be documented and handled explicitly.

Reporting coverage will be examined before constructing zero-count periods. Periods with unknown reporting status will not automatically be interpreted as periods without outbreaks.

Potential limitations include underreporting, changes in surveillance systems, geographic differences in reporting practices, and the absence of population or water-exposure denominators. Therefore, the analysis will focus on reported outbreak counts rather than population-level disease incidence or causal conclusions.

Expected Deliverables

The final project will consist of a functional R package and a publicly accessible pkgdown website containing two reproducible analytical vignettes.

Each vignette will provide documentation of data provenance, clearly defined research objectives, descriptive statistics, visualizations, statistical modeling, scientific interpretation, and a discussion of uncertainty and limitations.

All analyses will be implemented in R, with reproducible code and documented data-processing decisions.

  • CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
